summary: Defines two new DHCPv4 options that identify vendors by Enterprise Number. They are modeled on the IPv6 vendor options and remove the ambiguity that arises when a DHCP client represents more than one vendor.

eli5.summary: If a device is made of parts from several companies, the older form had room for only one company's name. These new options let it list each company by its registered number.

questions: what is a dhcp vendor class option
what is an enterprise number in dhcp
subtitle: Two DHCPv4 options that label each vendor's data with an IANA Enterprise Number, so several vendors can share one packet.

tldr.problem: DHCPv4 option 60 names one vendor and option 43 carries vendor data with no vendor label of its own, so a client that represents several vendors gets ambiguous results.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 3925 defines option 124 (vendor class) and option 125 (vendor-specific information). Each holds repeated blocks of an Enterprise Number, a length and that vendor's data.
tldr.outcome: Each vendor's data is interpreted on its own and no longer depends on a single option 60 value. The old options are unaffected and can still be used alongside the new ones.

today: RFC 3925 is a Proposed Standard from October 2004. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: The Ambiguity Problem
sections.content:
The DHCP protocol for IPv4 (RFC 2131) lets a client name its vendor type with option 60 and lets client and server swap vendor-specific information with option 43. Sending several copies of these options is not forbidden, but it creates ambiguity. Option 60 decides how option 43 is read, and option 43 carries no vendor identifier of its own.

There is a second problem. RFC 3396 requires multiple instances of the same option to be concatenated, so several copies of option 60 or 43 would not stay independent.

The RFC gives a real case. An implementation may need an industry-standard use of DHCPv4 and also the manufacturer's own options. Vendors of devices that follow CableLabs standards such as DOCSIS, CableHome and PacketCable face this, because those standards define an industry-specific use for options 60 and 43.
sections.eli5: The old way had room for only one company's name on a package. If the package held things from several companies, nobody could tell whose was whose.

sections.title: Supporting Multiple Vendor Instances
sections.content:
The two new options are modeled on the IPv6 vendor options in RFC 3315. The data of each option holds an enterprise number assigned by IANA, then an internal data length, then vendor-specific data. This sequence may repeat several times inside one option, once per vendor.

Because the combined vendor data can exceed 255 octets, both options are declared concatenation-requiring under RFC 3396. All instances together count as one long option. It can be split into smaller options on any convenient octet boundary, and splitting between vendor instances is allowed but not required.

The new options can be used in addition to the current vendor class and vendor information options, whose definitions are unaffected.
sections.eli5: Each company gets its own labeled section in one long list. If the list is too long for one envelope, it can be cut into several envelopes and glued back together.

sections.title: The Vendor-Identifying Vendor Class Option
sections.content:
A client may use the V-I Vendor Class option (OPTION_V-I_VENDOR_CLASS, code 124) to identify the vendor that made its hardware, the software in use, or an industry consortium the vendor belongs to. It may appear wherever option 60 may, except in DHCPNAK messages, and it is most meaningful in client-to-server messages (DHCPDISCOVER, DHCPREQUEST, DHCPINFORM).

After the option code and length, the option holds one or more blocks. Each has a 32-bit Enterprise Number, a one-octet data-len and opaque vendor-class-data. That data is a series of items describing the client's hardware configuration or capabilities, such as the operating system version or the installed memory.

Multiple instances MUST be concatenated as RFC 3396 requires. An Enterprise Number SHOULD occur only once across all instances, and behavior is undefined if it occurs more than once. Each number's information is treated independently.
sections.eli5: The client holds up a name tag for each company whose hardware or software it runs, plus a few notes about itself, like its software version.

sections.title: The Vendor-Specific Information Option
sections.content:
The V-I Vendor-specific Information option (OPTION_V-I_VENDOR_OPTS, code 125) lets clients and servers exchange vendor-specific data. Either side may send it, and a client need not send the vendor class option first, though that is a typical flow. It is allowed in DHCPDISCOVER, DHCPOFFER, DHCPREQUEST, DHCPACK and DHCPINFORM.

Its layout matches the class option: repeated blocks of Enterprise Number, data-len and option-data. The meaning of the data is defined by the vendor named in the Enterprise Number. The same rules apply: concatenate instances, and use each Enterprise Number only once.

The option-data MUST be a sequence of code/length/value fields in the same format as the DHCP options field. The sub-option codes belong to the vendor and are not managed by IANA. Codes 0 and 255 have no pre-defined interpretation or format.

A server that cannot interpret the vendor data MUST ignore it. A client that does not receive the vendor information it wanted SHOULD try to operate without it.
sections.eli5: Here the client and server pass notes written in each company's own private code. If you cannot read a company's code, you skip that note and carry on.

sections.title: IANA and Security Considerations
sections.content:
The option codes for OPTION_V-I_VENDOR_CLASS and OPTION_V-I_VENDOR_OPTS were assigned from the numbering space for public DHCP options defined in RFC 2939.

The RFC says it provides no security by itself and does not change existing security. If authenticity is needed for data carried in these options, the DHCP authentication and message integrity mechanism of RFC 3118 may be used.
sections.eli5: These options do not lock anything. If you need to be sure a note really came from the right sender, DHCP has a separate way to check.
